http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/31/autho.text: Nepal was burying on Monday some of the hundreds of bodies retrieved after a deadly, tsunami-like flood crashed through the Himalayan region, sweeping away villages and causing widespread destruction in its path.In south-central Nepal's Chitwan district, hundreds of victims were being buried while awaiting identification in hastily dug trenches serving as temporary graves, prompting accusations from locals that Hindu funeral traditions were being ignored.Government officials have noted that the measure is needed due to the severity of the situation, as the catastrophic floods are estimated to have killed at least 903 people, a number which could rise dramatically as 4,247 more are still reported missing.Some of the bodies that were buried were carried hundreds of kilometres downstream by the Bhotekoshi River from the flood's epicentre before being recovered in Chitwan.Distraught families have packed rescue stations and hospitals in search of their missing relatives, while others have faced the grim task of identifying bodies at overflowing morgues.Authorities carried out a temporary burial of about 100 victims on Saturday, officials said, as forensic teams struggled to cope. A convoy of vehicles carrying bodies entered a lush, forested area as an excavator dug a wide trench in the red earth while officials and media looked on.Anil Thapa, a police inspector coordinating the handling of the bodies, said another 50 bodies were having DNA samples taken ahead of their likely burial on Sunday.Limited forensic infrastructure and inadequate morgue capacity in the district further strained efforts to manage the overwhelming number of bodies recovered from the disaster, officials said.High humidity and sweltering heat accelerated decomposition, compounding the challenges as health experts warned that leaving the remains exposed could increase the risk of disease.As survivors grappled with the aftermath, criticism of the burials mounted. Some residents said the dead had waited days for their last rites and were denied dignity in death. Families still waiting to locate missing relatives and some public figures questioned whether authorities moved too quickly.The issue is particularly sensitive in Nepal, a predominantly Hindu nation where the dead are traditionally cremated. Ruby Chaudhary, who has two missing relatives, said the burials should not proceed without families’ consent.“The dead deserve to be treated with dignity,” she said. “Our tradition is to cremate them on the riverbank, surrounded by their immediate family.”“People are worried that this could be a permanent burial, but it is only temporary management,” said Thapa. “If someone is able to verify the identity later using the available information, they can take back the body and perform the appropriate funeral rites.”Amrit Bahadur Rai, Nepal’s foreign secretary, said the temporary burial of unidentified bodies was carried out in line with internationally accepted disaster-management protocols, including those of the International Committee of the Red Cross.“Families can match records later, and will be allowed to exhume (the remains later) for necessary rituals,” Rai said at a press briefing in the capital Kathmandu.

Photograph: Tomer Appelbaum/AP View image in fullscreen Yaniv Hayoun, a passenger on the flydubai aircraft, is welcomed at Ben Gurion international airport. Photograph: Tomer Appelbaum/AP Flydubai plane incident Motive behind flydubai cockpit stabbing unknown as international investigation opens Benjamin Netanyahu says too early to tell who may have been behind plane incident as carrier halts all flights to Israel William Christou and Jonathan Yerushalmy Thu 1 Oct 2026 06.59 EDT First published on Thu 1 Oct 2026 00.55 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The motive, background and affiliation of the Omani co-pilot who stabbed his captain in an apparent attempt to crash an Israel-bound flight from Dubai remains unknown, as international teams open investigations into the incident. Israeli passengers intervened to stop the attack on Wednesday, restraining the co-pilot, while a reserve crew in the plane was able to stabilise the plummeting plane and ultimately land it safely in Saudi Arabia. A ‘hero’ pilot, plumber and dentist among those who saved flydubai flight to Israel Read more The plane had more than 170 people onboard and Israeli officials praised the bravery of those who intervened, announcing that four of the Israeli passengers would receive a “heroism” award for preventing a potential disaster. Saudi investigators, who initially detained the co-pilot upon landing, were cooperating with the United Arab Emirates , the US, Oman and Israel to try to determine the attacker’s motive, a regional official familiar with the investigation said. “All possible scenarios, from terrorism to mental disorders, are being looked into. Nothing is ruled out for now,” they told the Associated Press. Benjamin Netanyahu said that it was still not known who may have been ultimately behind the apparent attempted attack. The Israeli prime minister told Fox News it was “too early to say” if there was any Iranian involvement. “We’ll get to the root of this attacker, whether he had accomplices, whether Iran was behind it. I think we’ll find out very soon,” Netanyahu said. It came just days after Netanyahu warned of an unspecified security threat to Israel that could come during its October election. The Israeli military had said before the incident it had no specific intelligence of an imminent threat, while the opposition leader Yair Lapid said that a security briefing on Tuesday night included no mention of a related threat. Map of flight path Other Israeli officials, including the defence minister, Israel Katz, and the ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, suggested the incident was a “terror attack”, with the Israeli foreign ministry briefing its diplomats that the attack was against Israel and its relationship with the UAE. Danon told Fox News that Israel had “no doubt it was a terror attack from a radical individual”, but said that until now investigators had not established any link to a specific organisation or state. Donald Trump suggested the co-pilot was “perhaps a terrorist or perhaps a whack job”, while telling reporters at the White House that he and Netanyahu had spoken at length. Netanyahu also spoke to the president of the UAE, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, who agreed to Israel’s involvement in the investigation. Flydubai said its flights to and from Israel would be suspended while the investigation took place and urged all parties “to refrain from premature speculation while authorities gather the facts”. 1:03 Passenger recalls putting pilot in ‘chokehold’ after stabbing on Israel-bound flight - video The UAE announced on Thursday that it would be conducting its own investigation of the incident, which started about two and a half hours after takeoff from Dubai. It said its investigators had begun to look into the attacker’s motive and if he had any links to any “terrorist purpose”. Passengers said they saw a knife-wielding man – apparently the Omani co-pilot – putting the captain of the plane on the floor, after which the plane began to plummet. The wounded pilot, Smit Machchhar, an Indian national, managed to send out an emergency signal and open the cockpit door, allowing passengers to enter and stop the plane’s descent. A video shared by the prime minister’s office showed one passenger, Yaniv Hayoun, a plumber, speaking to Netanyahu at length about how the events onboard played out. Hayoun told the prime minister he and other passengers heard screaming and felt the air pressure change as the plane dived before they forced their way into the cockpit and found the attacker at the instrument panel. “I grabbed the attacker, put him in a chokehold, and dragged him out first,” Hayoun said during the meeting with Netanyahu after the plane had landed safely and the passengers were flown to Israel. Machchhar was widely praised for his bravery, with Netanyahu and the Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi, hailing him as a hero. India’s ambassador to the UAE met the wounded captain’s family and briefed them on his recovery, the Indian consulate in the UAE said. Machchhar was being treated in a hospital in Tabuk. “Captain Smit Machchhar is a HERO,” Modi said, in a post on social media. “In the face of the gravest danger and despite being seriously injured, he showed immense courage and an unwavering resolve to protect the lives of others.” Explore more on these topics Flydubai plane incident Israel United Arab Emirates Middle East and north Africa Benjamin Netanyahu Air transport Saudi Arabia news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Should cockpits stay locked from the inside? https://www.dw.com/en/finland-probes-sus.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5NbCe Officials are speaking of a "significant" number of break-ins and attempted intrusions at the homes of several MPs [FILE: March 2023] Image: Heikki Saukkomaa/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement Finnish police are investigating a series of suspected break-ins at the homes of members of parliament, officials announced on Thursday. Finland 's Prime Minister Petteri Orpo was asked by a reporter if a foreign power could be behind the suspected intrusions, and he replied that it was "very possible... quite possible in these times." "If someone tries to destabilize Finland, our sense of security, or our support for example for Ukraine, it has the opposite effect. It strengthens our unity," he added. Meanwhile, Finnish President Alexander Stubb stated, "An attack against a member of parliament is an attack against democracy." What do we know about break-ins? After the media reported on the alleged intrusions, speaker of parliament Jussi Halla-aho confirmed that parliament had been made aware of a "significant" number of break-ins and attempted intrusions at the homes of several politicians. "I cannot comment precisely on the number of suspected cases known to us, but in any event, it is significant," Halla-aho said at a press conference. He added, however, that the known cases had occurred over a longer period of time, with the first believed to have taken place about a year ago. Halla-aho also emphasized that, at this point, no information is available about the motive or the perpetrator. Paula Risikko, the deputy speaker who leads the parliamentary security group, said she was informed of the suspicions last week. She added that the Helsinki police had been tasked with the initial stage of the investigation. A night in Finland's largest underground defense bunker To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video MPs advised to keep an eye out Earlier this week, newspaper Ilta-Sanomat reported that MPs had been warned of potential break-ins and that the newspaper was aware of at least two home intrusions. All members of parliament were told to keep an eye out, report any suspicious activity, and file police reports if necessary. Helsinki police confirmed that a preliminary inquiry had been opened. "The inquiry is at an early stage, and the police have nothing further to comment on at this time," it said. Since the Kremlin began its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Finland has been on high alert . The Nordic country, which shares a 1,340-kilometer (830-mile) border with Russia, abandoned its decades-long policy of military non-alignment and joined NATO in April 2023. Finland previously accused Moscow of "hybrid warfare" and orchestrating a surge of migrants at their shared border in 2023. The Kremlin denied the allegations. https://www.politico.eu/article/sam-altm.text: Pour le PDG d’OpenAI Sam Altman, il subsiste une différence fondamentale de vision entre son entreprise et son concurrent Anthropic en matière de réglementation de l’intelligence artificielle. Les avantages de cette technologie justifient d’accepter certains risques, a-t-il estimé dans une interview exclusive accordée à Decoded by POLITICO, ajoutant que l’IA devait rester largement accessible au grand public. “Je pense qu’il y a un réel fossé”, a souligné Sam Altman auprès de Brendan Bordelon, coauteur de Decoded et journaliste senior spécialisé dans la tech chez POLITICO. Interrogé sur ce qu’il différencie plus spécifiquement son entreprise de celle de Dario Amodei, il a répondu : “Nous pensons que le monde devrait accepter que certaines choses négatives se produisent face aux bénéfices de cette technologie.” Anthropic a longtemps été considérée comme la plus fervente défenseure de la réglementation de l’IA au sein du secteur, une position qui, jusqu’à récemment, contrastait avec l’approche plus souple prônée par OpenAI. Mais les divergences politiques entre ces deux géants de l’intelligence artificielle se sont atténuées ces derniers mois, la maison mère de ChatGPT soutenant désormais des règles plus strictes, alors que ses modèles ont défrayé la chronique pour avoir piraté des sites de manière autonome. Advertisement Advertisement Sam Altman a approuvé l’appel lancé le mois dernier par Dario Amodei à ralentir le développement des modèles d’IA les plus avancés. Son entreprise a même emboîté le pas à Anthropic en soutenant de nouvelles lois d’Etats fédérés américains qui imposent des exigences de sécurité plus strictes que celles qu’OpenAI avait précédemment défendues — ce qui marque un léger revirement par rapport à sa stratégie antérieure en la matière . Par ailleurs, ses lobbyistes ont récemment apporté leur soutien à une proposition bipartisane de la Chambre des représentants qui obligerait les principales entreprises du secteur à accueillir des auditeurs indépendants chargés d’évaluer la sécurité de leurs modèles. Malgré cette convergence, Sam Altman a tenté de distinguer la position de son entreprise en matière de réglementation de celle de Dario Amodei, rappelant les accusations de capture réglementaires contre Anthropic, formulées par des conseillers tech du président Donald Trump. “Je ne suis pas d’accord, mais je comprends le point de vue de ceux qui se disent : ‘Cette technologie va devenir tellement puissante, et elle est tellement dangereuse, qu’un seul laboratoire à San Francisco devrait en disposer et veiller à ce qu’il n’arrive rien de grave, tout en trouvant le moyen d’en répartir les bénéfices’”, a exposé Sam Altman. Pour lui, c’est un “compromis totalement inacceptable” qui va à l’encontre de la “position plus souple en matière réglementaire” défendue par OpenAI. “Je ne ferai pas le compromis de dire : ‘Nous veillerons à ce qu’il n’y ait pas de piratages majeurs, pas d’utilisation abusive de cette technologie, zéro escroquerie [ou] toute autre chose négative qui pourrait se produire’”, a poursuivi le patron de l’éditeur de ChatGPT. “Car je pense que les gens feront énormément plus — d’un ordre de grandeur supérieur — de bonnes choses que de mauvaises.” Le PDG d’OpenAI a ajouté ne pas croire aux “risques véritablement catastrophiques”, notamment à la possibilité d’“une grave perte de contrôle face à l’IA”. Interrogé à ce sujet, un porte-parole d’Anthropic a répondu que les “propositions réglementaires [de l’entreprise] ne s’appliquent qu’aux modèles de pointe”. La société a également fait référence à un échange sur les réseaux sociaux en août entre Dario Amodei et un gestionnaire d’investissements, dans lequel il répondait aux critiques concernant la captation réglementaire et les répercussions sur les petites entreprises. Advertisement Advertisement “Anthropic a toujours formulé ses propositions politiques avec beaucoup de prudence”, soulignait Dario Amodei à l’époque. “Nous nous efforçons vraiment de présenter des propositions qui désavantagent (freinent) les entreprises d’IA de pointe tout en *favorisant* leurs concurrents plus petits.” L’interview de Sam Altman, publiée lundi dans le premier numéro de Decoded et dans le podcast quotidien qui l’accompagne, a également abordé le nouvel accord sur l’IA de Donald Trump avec les géants de la tech, ainsi que son initiative de la rebaptiser “superintelligence” ; la vague d’incidents de piratage autonome perpétrés par des modèles d’OpenAI et la question de savoir si l’entreprise devrait engager sa responsabilité juridique ; l’opinion de Sam Altman sur l’argent du secteur de l’IA qui inonde la politique américaine ; l’influence des “altruistes efficaces” au sein d’OpenAI ; ainsi que son point de vue sur des acteurs politiques de premier plan, notamment le président français Emmanuel Macron et le gouverneur de Californie Gavin Newsom. Decoded by POLITICO — une émission réalisée par Brendan Bordelon, Christine Mui, Calder McHugh et Sam Sutton — s’appuie sur le travail d’une cinquantaine de journalistes de POLITICO à travers le monde pour traiter non seulement de l’avenir de la tech, mais aussi des personnalités, des débats politiques et des luttes qui la façonne. Abonnez-vous à la newsletter et au podcast . Cet article a d’abord été publié par POLITICO en anglais, puis a été édité en français par Jean-Christophe Catalon.
